Vox reported in May 2024 that OpenAI's exit agreements barred ex-staff from criticising the company for life, at the risk of losing vested equity. OpenAI told Vox it had never cancelled anyone's vested equity. Days later, Bloomberg reported, OpenAI told former staff it would not cancel vested units, would release them from non-disparagement agreements unless the clause was mutual, and would remove the language from exit paperwork.
In May 2024, OpenAI said it would not cancel vested equity over criticism. That statement does not establish protection against withheld pay or blocked equity sales.

Its Jan 2026 policy says staff are always free to report concerns to an outside authority, without telling OpenAI first. In 2024, whistleblowers alleged restrictive agreements hindered SEC reporting; OpenAI said its policy protected disclosures, TechCrunch reported.
Published a Raising Concerns Policy in Oct 2024 and an expanded version in Jan 2026.
Anonymous Integrity Line and a no-retaliation rule. Run by OpenAI's Compliance team; AI safety concerns can be escalated to the board's Safety and Security Committee.

Contracts aren't public. The Register reported on 2 Oct 2026 that OpenAI had dismissed three staff, saying they mishandled sensitive company information. Some of it was allegedly shared with an outside AI evaluation group. OpenAI says the dismissals weren't about raising safety concerns.
Vox reported in 2024 that even admitting the old exit agreement existed counted as a breach. Current terms aren't public.

Andreas Kirsch, a former Google DeepMind research scientist, posted on X a clause from the Confidentiality and Proprietary Information Agreement he signed with Google in the UK in 2024. It says that "at all times during employment and after the termination of employment" staff must not make "any statement" to anyone "criticising or disparaging Google". He says it has no exemption for protected disclosures. Google employees also told the BBC that their contracts stop staff publicly criticising the company, and a research engineer who had just resigned said: "In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life." Google's statement to the BBC, as published, said staff have dedicated channels to raise concerns and that it prohibits retaliation. It didn't mention employment contracts. FLI's July 2026 index, partly using Google's private survey answers, gave Google 9 out of 10 for an explicit statement that NDAs and non-disparagement agreements can't stop safety-related whistleblowing.

FLI's July 2026 review, using evidence up to 3 June, found no public whistleblowing policy. Google's Code of Conduct describes reporting channels and protection from retaliation.
Google says it has dedicated channels to raise concerns and anti-retaliation policies. Staff told the BBC people fear retaliation.

In July 2026, The Midas Project reported no public whistleblowing policy. It reported that xAI's June framework revision removed earlier language on whistleblower protections and anonymous reporting. The December 2025 framework contained those commitments.

In March 2025, at Meta's request, an arbitrator issued an interim order temporarily barring a former Facebook director of global public policy from promoting her memoir, Careless People, while the arbitration continued. The arbitrator found Meta had a valid argument that she may have breached the non-disparagement agreement she signed when she left in 2017. Meta called the book a mix of out-of-date claims and false accusations. Meta's current terms aren't public.

FLI's July 2026 review, using evidence up to 3 June, found Meta's full whistleblowing policy was not public. Its October framework says a policy exists and further AI reporting procedures are being developed; it does not publish the full policy.
